review.reason: Read primary task design, behavioural and fMRI results, network-lesion predictions, ultrasound intervention, discussion, participant selection, blinding, stimulation and statistical methods. Explains inference from a learned relational structure while distinguishing neural correlations, model predictions and intervention evidence. Preserves the null overall-accuracy result, small selected sample, lack of preregistration and possible connected-network effects.

item.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
item.headline: The hippocampus helps people use a pattern to infer a missing relationship
item.authors: Deng Pan, Simone D’Ambrogio, Naomi Kingston, Miruna Rascu, Pranav Sankhe, Shuyi Luo, Miriam C. Klein-Flügge, Ali Mahmoodi and Matthew F. S. Rushworth
item.summary: If four characters always form two pairs, discovering one pair tells you something about the other. In a football-themed prediction game, participants used this kind of structure to adapt when pairings changed. Brain scans in 36 people linked that structure to hippocampal activity. In a separate group of 20, ultrasound targeting the hippocampus reduced a behavioural measure of structure-based inference compared with stimulation at a control site. Overall prediction accuracy did not show a detectable change. The result supports a role for the hippocampus and its connected network in this specific kind of learning, rather than showing that stimulation erased memories or reasoning generally.

evidence.question: Does the human hippocampus help learners infer changing relationships from an abstract structure learned previously?
evidence.method: Participants learned probabilistic transitions among four characters arranged in two pairs, then predicted shots in a game with changing pairings and shot preferences. The study combined fMRI in 36 participants, computational models and a separate counterbalanced within-person ultrasound experiment in 20 participants. Each person received hippocampal and white-matter control-site stimulation in sessions at least one week apart. Two additional groups of 40 completed behavioural experiments without stimulation, including one with revised instructions.
evidence.limitations: The ultrasound sample consisted of selected healthy adults aged 19–33; 32 were initially scanned, 23 met simulation-based targeting criteria and 20 completed both sessions. Participants were blinded, but the experimenter was not, and none of the experiments was preregistered. Inference was estimated from choices in a constrained task. Stimulation can affect connected regions, and no detectable overall-accuracy effect is not proof of no such effect.

explainer.finding: Hippocampal stimulation reduced how strongly both direct pair experience and information about the other pair guided behaviour, especially early in learning. The inference effect was reduced relative to control stimulation (Cohen’s d = −0.89; 95% confidence interval −1.41 to −0.36). Learning individual characters’ shot preferences and overall prediction accuracy showed no statistically detectable changes.
explainer.method: The key comparison separated seeing a pair directly from inferring it after seeing the other pair. Brain imaging tested whether activity patterns reflected that structure. A recurrent neural network generated predictions about disrupting structure representations; the separate ultrasound experiment then tested whether targeting the hippocampus changed human behaviour relative to an active control site.
explainer.meaning: Knowing that A pairs with B lets you infer that C pairs with D when the rule is two pairs among four characters. You do not need to observe every connection from scratch. The experiment tests how a learned pattern can help fill in missing information when the particular characters or pairings change.
explainer.limits: A network simulation is not a biological account of how hippocampal neurons work. The stimulation result supports causal involvement of the hippocampus and possibly its broader network, not an isolated brain region responsible for all inference. Small selected samples and this artificial task limit generalization to everyday learning; this was not a treatment or memory-improvement trial.
